covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

electronAffinity.note: PubChem lists no electron affinity for this element.

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('2.8 milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('5.6×10⁻⁶ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: meteoritic (CI-chondrite) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Gordon, P. (1949). Journal of Applied Physics 20, 908.

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, beryllium content, 2025 (USGS: 430 metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, annual average unit value, beryllium-copper master alloy, dollars per kilogram of contained beryllium [Beryllium], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

origin.note: Paper Sect. 3.5: 'Be and B are supposed to be produced by cosmic rays [Prantzos et al. 1993], which is not included in our model either.' Empty box in Fig. 39. Value is the paper's qualitative statement, not a modelled fraction.

splitting.note: Zero-field A0 from Penning-trap hyperfine-Zeeman spectroscopy (Shiga, Itano, Bollinger 2011), extrapolated over the diamagnetic shift. Splitting derived as 2|A0|. Negative A: inverted structure (F=1 above F=2).

gamma.note: Γ/2π from NIST's A_ki = 1.129e+08 s⁻¹ (accuracy class AAA), taking the upper level to decay only on this line; where it has other decay channels the true linewidth is slightly larger.

laserCooling.note: Only stable isotope. Wavelength: NIST observed value. first_cooled = the paper the Olmschenk ion catalog lists as first 'trapped/laser cooled'.

biology.note: Not known to be essential for plants or for humans.

history.nameOrigin: From beryl (Greek beryllos), the gemstone that contains it.
history.symbolNote: Long called glucinium (symbol Gl), after the sweet taste of its salts; IUPAC chose the name beryllium in 1949.
history.note: CIAAW dates Vauquelin's discovery to 1797. Wöhler and Bussy obtained the metal independently, both by reducing the chloride with potassium.

prose.text: Beryllium is a light, stiff, steel-grey metal of the alkaline-earth group, found in the mineral beryl, of which emerald and aquamarine are coloured varieties. Because X-rays pass through it easily, thin beryllium sheets serve as windows in X-ray tubes, and gold-coated beryllium forms the mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope. Beryllium has only one stable isotope, beryllium-9, whose nucleus has spin 3/2; the lighter beryllium-8 falls apart into two helium nuclei almost instantly, a bottleneck stars must overcome to make carbon. Its four electrons fill the 1s and 2s orbitals, giving [He] 2s² and the ground term ¹S₀.
